records.title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
records.author: mday404
records.storyText:
a ball will fall. trade on where it lands.

I made this game! Some technical details:

The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome.

There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky.

Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.

records.title: Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
records.author: rxliuli
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I made a small macOS utility for my own iOS simulator workflow.

I kept running into two annoyances: getting config files in and out of a simulator is clunky (digging into CoreSimulator UUID folders or running simctl), and on the iPhone Duo simulator I couldn't even drag and drop images onto the window at all.

SimDrop puts every running iOS simulator in Finder's sidebar (under Locations) with two folders:

- Downloads/ (Files app > On My iPhone > Downloads) - Photos and Videos/ (the simulator's Photos library)

Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal under ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop-SimDrop/.

A couple of caveats up front: - Dragging moves files by default (same as iCloud Drive, because it uses File Provider on the startup volume)—hold Option to copy. - macOS 15+ and iOS simulators only (not physical devices).

It's free, open source (GPL-3.0), signed and notarized, and installable via Homebrew:

  brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop
Just sharing in case others run into the same friction—feedback or PRs welcome!

records.title: Show HN: Europe Instead – find the European version of the tools you use
records.author: RafaelRoman
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Rafael. Europe Instead is a directory of European-made software: https://europeinstead.com

I built it because every time we needed a new tool at my startup, Upgrid, I ended up doing the same research again: who actually owns this company, where is the data hosted, who are the subprocessors. After doing that enough times I got tired of it and started writing it down properly. The existing "EU alternatives" lists didn't help much, because most check one thing, the legal seat. A company registered in Berlin can be owned by a US parent, run on AWS us-east-1, and send your data to a dozen US subprocessors. That is a different risk from a Berlin company on Hetzner.

So every tool gets two separate answers:

- Origin score (0-100): how European the company is, from five parts: legal entity, ownership and control, operations, data residency, and openness. Weights are published on the method page.

- Exposure level (1-5): which jurisdictions can legally reach the core customer data, based on where it is hosted and who the subprocessors are.

Every fact links to the page it came from, with the check date and usually a quoted line. If we couldn't find evidence, the fact is shown as "not verified" and scores zero, rather than being guessed. Right now that is about a quarter of all facts, which tells you something about how little vendors disclose.

Some details:

- 1,818 tools from 33 countries, across 212 categories, mapped as alternatives to 453 US products (Calendly, Typeform, Intercom, Google Analytics, and so on).

- Vendors can correct their record by form or email. Corrections are reviewed by a person and logged in a public change history.

- Listing is free and unconditional. No backlink required, and rankings can't be bought. If I ever sell sponsored slots, they sit above the ranked list with their own numbering and a "Sponsored" label; the ranking below always starts at 1 and doesn't move.

A few things you might find useful:

- "Alternative to X" pages: name the tool you use today and see the European ones that do the same job.

- Stacks: a full European set of tools for a small company, one per job.

- A read-only API and an MCP server, so you can ask an AI assistant for a European alternative and get the sourced record back (https://europeinstead.com/developers).

- A free badge vendors can embed. It links to their live record and has no tracking.

What I'd like from you: tell me where the data is wrong, and tell me where the method is wrong. In particular I'm unsure how to treat the UK and Switzerland (included, country always shown so you can apply a stricter definition), and whether "uses AWS Frankfurt" should count against a tool as much as it does now.

records.title: Show HN: Play with VST/CLAP instruments and effects in the browser
records.author: mrmufungo
records.storyText:
For awhile now, I thought it'd be cool to be able to try out various instrument / effect plugins in the browser without having to download them and open up a DAW. I saw this as a challenge, so I spent the last few weeks working on a demo app.

One thing I wanted to avoid was making this obscenely costly. Plugins can be CPU and memory intensive, so larger EC2 instances would be needed. However, running even one of these continuously is very expensive, let alone a fleet of them. I initially tried working with a single instance and attempting a sort of preemptive scheduling / context switching, but this quickly fell apart: the signal chain between sessions would become polluted, and it was extremely brittle.

It's around this time that I found that EC2 spot instances can be considerably cheaper. With aggressive session cleanup and instance lifetime limits, I could probably keep this doable.

Limitations:

* Max session time is an hour.

* Only a single signal chain is supported, with an instrument being the root node and one or more effects after it. Parallel chains are technically supported by the engine, but I decided against implementing it in the browser for simplicity.

* Plugins marked with "demo" are paid products with a publicly available demo version. These demos will emit crackles or dropouts, so if you like the plugin, consider purchasing it from the developer.

* Snapshots allow you to freeze your graph (plugin order, parameter values) at a specific time, and also share your snapshot with others. Currently, snapshots are stored in memory only, as I didn't want to over engineer a durable store for a demo app. Also, once your session is over, snapshots are deleted along with it.

* Some plugins may work better than others.

Implementation details:

* Sessions provision EC2 spot instances, or grab hibernating instances from a pool if one is available.

* Each EC2 instance runs a worker binary that maintains a graph of nodes, with each node being a Podman container that communicates with the worker via Unix sockets.

* Podman images include WINE and yabridge for VST3 only plugins; container initialization time is kept low thanks to fuse-overlayfs preventing redundant copying of the WINE prefix.

* Each container has a small VST/CLAP host that reads input via the control socket; output can be GUI frames or audio blocks.

* Output is streamed over a WebSocket, with WebAudio for scheduling playback

records.title: Show HN: Graphvein – Trace calls to handlers and tables across repos, no LLM
records.author: saptashwa
records.storyText:
As I started developing more projects using AI assistance over this year, I started facing the problem that most people have voiced against using AI - the overall architecture/design of the project becomes known only to the agent, and you lose control of the project. I thought what if we could map the architecture, calls, routes, table schemas etc. from the code - that is how this project was born in October.

Now I searched a little bit and came upon a few different projects, but none of them did what I wanted to do - at least in full. And quite a few of them used LLMs themselves to do that - which could be plausibly wrong (hallucinated) and non deterministic. Therefore I have built this over the last 2 months to create a base which:

1. Extracts routes, table schema, request and response bodies across HTTP requests, Tauri calls etc.

2. Gives you an overview of the architecture which you can dive into including how each handler is linked to routes or tables - it works in both directions in a fan out mode from any layer

3. Gives you an overview of the table schema extracted from the project and how they link together

4. An OpenAPI spec extracted from the project, with a try-it mode like Swagger

5. Change impact and what changing a particular piece of code might impact across the stack

6. It supports zero or more frontends, and one or more backends together in a project and how they all link together

It supports TypeScript / JavaScript (Express, Next.js, Angular, Angular HttpClient, hey-api, fetch, axios, Prisma, Drizzle, Sequelize, TypeORM, Orval and Supabase clients), Python (FastAPI, SQLModel), Go (net/http, chi, gin, GORM), and Rust (Axum, Tauri commands, Diesel). Database support is for SQL (tested with Postgres) and Java, C# and Dart get structure only in this preview release. It also has a read-only MCP server which agents can use to get Graphvein-verified information and not have to grep around files to figure things out.

No data leaves your computer (other than the try it environments you configure yourself), and everything is done locally, without any LLM (not even local LLMs). I do plan on adding LLM support in the future, but only building upon this base - for gap-filling, generation of wikis and other features which can use the deterministic core and build upon it. And it will remain opt-in even then.

Please feel free to check out the GitHub repo or the website (https://graphvein.com/) to get more details. Please let me know which language support/framework would make this more appealing to use, or if you have any other feature requests.

potluck is a site where everyone brings 5 picks to the table: a YouTube video, a song, a podcast, a book, a movie or show, a game, a Wikipedia article, or a paper. You can see what people on your guest list brought, up to 150 of them.

I wanted to go against the grain of algorithmic feeds and find more thoughtful ways of consuming media. Ideally, we would get recommendations from people we trust through in person conversations, or less ideally through calls and group chats. Realistically, these conversations are scattered and easy to lose. A dedicated, central place for peer recommendations on fixed rails removes some friction while keeping the signal of trust alive.

The design decisions are also motivated by minimizing cost and complexity: only supported links for allowlisted domains, strict limits on picks, guest lists, and changes, and everything runs on one Cloudflare Worker with D1 and static pages.

records.title: Show HN: Open-Sourced Code Mode to Cut ~60% of My Rust Agent's Token Burn
records.author: legend-of-alan
records.storyText:
For those who are tracking, Anthropic released an announcement last week about their experimental code mode for Claude Code, claiming some bonkers token savings when it comes to tool calls (95% on some workloads(1)). I haven't benchmarked it myself, but independent studies come in somewhere closer to 60~70% savings (2), but I digress. TLDR; I built an open-source version for the community.

Context: I'm writing an AI RPG engine called Spookery, and I immediately wanted to try this technique for myself when I heard of it. Agent deployment is currently dominated by token costs, especially during tool calling (single prompt generating tens or hundreds of tool calls). Unfortunately, it looks like the only ones who are doing this seriously are big agentic products like Claude Code and Codex. So, I thought it'd be fun to try it myself and bring it to you all!

The idea of Code Mode is simple but powerful. Instead of passing back tool call results back to the LLM one at a time, let the LLM batch calls by letting it write a short script using your tools. Basically taking 30 trips to the grocery store for 30 items and turning it into one trip to the store with a list in-hand.

There's a few near-ish open-source options, but they used TypeScript backends, we're a little boilerplate heavy, and I wanted to have something a little faster and Rust friendly for my game engine. Pydantic's Monty seemed a good candidate--their self-reports are around 5x faster on execution and 100x faster on startup (3). I wouldn't take the numbers to the bank, but it's written on a Rust framework and the python backend is entirely built from Rust too.

Anyway, I had a couple of days off unexpectedly. So, I went temporarily insane and built a Rust tool to bring code mode to the greater community for free. In enough days to fit on one hand (and just as many hours of sleep), I came up with the implementation linked. I call it Ghost Mode. It's MIT licensed. It's a drop-in for your agent that already makes traditional tool calls. With ~20 lines of setup, you can convert your existing agent to a Code Mode agent.

I hope you get something out of this, and maybe I can save you some money. Considering how limiting token economics are right now, I think this could be a game changer for the industry. If there's interest, I can imagine we can build also add some great new features, language compatibility, and other great things. Thanks for reading :)

Sources: (1) https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/11/17/anthropic-claude-cod... (2) https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19123 (3) https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/get-started/

records.title: Show HN: Status page for your AI bots
records.author: kirillzubovsky
records.storyText:
Do you run multiple AI agents in terminals, in bots, concurrently remotely and locally?

Does it get overwhelming to know which agent is actually doing what, and where they are in their progress?

Meet https://statuspan.com

Open source, free, no strings attached, StatusPan is a quick local "departures board" for you and your agents. There's virtually no setup; just point your agents at the website, they install StatusPan and start pushing notification to it.

If you're working on one machine, that's all you need. If you're doing multiple machines, your agents will install a Cloudflare relay and sync through there.

I made this because I routinely run 10+ agents; some run on my Mac (in terminal and via Grok Bot), others run DGX Spark, and others are remote on a Hetzner server. At some point I couldn't tell who is actually doing what anymore, and needed a quick way to sync them all.

Now I just check StatupsPan, and only follow up with agents that are clearly stuck or failed.

If you find this helpful, hit me up on X (kirillzubovsky) and let me know. Thanks, hope it helps, and Happy Thanksgiving!

records.title: Show HN: Blur – a Mac app that hides secrets during screen sharing
records.author: mldbk
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

We built Blur for a moment you’ll recognize. You’re sharing screen on the call and open some app or file to show something, and accidentally discover that you also demo your API tokens.

Blur detects credentials as they appear and blurs just that part of the screen. The rest stays readable, so you can keep walking someone through the file. You can also hide entire apps from the screen share.

Detection runs entirely on your Mac. We use CoreML to run MobileNetV4 on Apple’s Neural Engine. Your screen content stays on your machine. Blur doesn’t ask for a username, an ID, or any other personal information. It only connects to the network to check for app updates. There is optional support for Jev-like networks, but it is disabled by default.

If you try it, we’d love to hear how it works for you.

records.title: Show HN: I posted a read-later-to-paper app here in 2020. Here's what happened
records.author: yorgos_kats
records.storyText:
Six years ago I posted "Turn your read later folder into a physical book" here (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=24690310) and went to watch a movie. I’ve been lurking in HN but didn’t really think much of it. Soon enough, people put all sorts of articles in our engine, commenting in the thread, sharing stories. I was definitely not prepared for this.

The idea seemed to resonate, or at least the problem did, so we got excited and built the full thing. And when we eventually launched, people ordered books and seemed to enjoy the reading experience, but it quickly became clear this wasn't going to turn into a habit. It was aspirational, maybe cool, but it didn’t solve the actual problem, which is when you decide you want to read something properly, you need to get off the feed. So lots of books have been in bedside tables instead of reading later folders, as the intent didn’t match the delivery.

The people who stuck around actually used it as a print button - curating reading experiences and when they wanted to invest time in reading, printed at home (or at staples) and did just that.

But Screenbreak wasn’t getting any meaningful traction, so we put it on autopilot and focused on other things. But when AI came around, I started thinking more about what we should build now that we weren’t able back then, and what we would do differently knowing what we'd learned?

The first thing I wanted to check is how good our engine could become with minimal effort. Our latest version on Zyte's article extraction benchmark (https://github.com/scrapinghub/article-extraction-benchmark), scored 0.896 (not bad). So we split the benchmark in half and tuned our engine in one half, and it reached 0.96 for this half. But on the other half, it scored 0.924, so there was a bit more work to do to reach readability (0.947) or trafilatura (0.958).

But we knew extraction was half of the struggle. The other half is typesetting. How you handle images, captions, tables and page breaks, across different designs. And with AI allowing us to work with Javascript more, we ported our typesetting rules and rebuilt the extraction engine around Mozilla's Readability, so it could run in your browser, and get those speed gains as well, on top of a higher baseline. With our extraction rules around it, we're at 0.957 (almost as trafilatura), and the typesetting rules sit on top of that.

With that working, we started thinking about what the product should actually be this time around. And we decided to focus on the simplest action, what we wanna call the print button of the web. No account, free, instantly accessible.

But we also knew a big part of the pain was the read later folders sitting there. So instead of building new workflows, we tried to build as simply as possible around existing workflows. Import the bookmarks that matter from your browser or send your newsletters directly. And as the pile grows longer, maybe use your agent to sift through it and propose a reading experience by asking ”build a 45’ booklet of good science reading”. And if e-ink is your thing, you can send it to your Kindle.

We haven’t gone back full time, but it's a fun way to keep building on the side with speed :)

records.title: Show HN: No-equipment workout generator with 3D-to-2D SVG figures
records.author: davidnashdev
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I built* HIIT Builder (https://hiitbuilder.app) because I don't want to get fat. Truly I could just stop there.

But for more context, I got tired of hunting for YouTube workout videos that have both good routines and decent music. Turns out most YT workout creators, even the massive ones who could afford a license, have terrible music. So, fk it, I'll build my own workout generator and play my own Spotify playlists instead.

So far workouts have been completed across 13 countries (US, Iraq, Bangladesh, Austria, France, Germany, Brazil, Ukraine, Turkey, Netherlands, Spain, Chile, Australia), and someone in the Faroe Islands, either physically or maybe just their VPN, started one too.

A few technical details that might be interesting to my fellow nerds here:

After a few ugly first prototypes for the stick figures, I ended up using the strategy of modeling every animation as a compact 34-number pose vector (joint angles, abduction, etc.) like a 3D skeleton, then projecting it to a 2D SVG. That way any move can be rendered at any angle without having to re-do any major work.

For workout order, instead of pure random shuffles the routine builder runs simulated annealing over a fixed standing/floor block shape. This makes it so that trips to the floor are limited and muscle groups are rotated logically. Rest time is actually rest instead of using that time to get up or get down off the floor constantly.

Since one of my main concerns was bringing your own music, there are no audio files at all. I did add countdown beeps though with synthesized chonky square waves so they cut through Spotify.

*Full disclosure: Using 'built' nowadays is a dividing term lol. I used AI to write all the code for it. And while I've spent many hours reviewing and tweaking poses over and over until the form cues actually looked right, a few of the moves still have noticeable quirks that AI is bad at noticing. If you spot any weird ones let me know.

records.title: Show HN: Targeted Mutation Testing – Observation-guided mutation testing tool
records.author: tk6879
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I built a mutation testing tool that takes a different approach from the conventional one. I'm calling it Targeted Mutation Testing.

As AI coding has become more common, mutation testing has become more important. It has helped me a lot personally. But ever since I first learned about it, I've kept wondering if there was a smarter way to do it.

Targeted Mutation Testing observes a single test run and generates targeted mutants from what it sees.

Of course, observation-guided rules have their own limits, so you can also combine them with classic mutation rules when you want more coverage.

This post links to the Rust implementation, which I built first. I also built a JS/TS implementation:

https://github.com/t-k/targeted-mutation-ts

What's interesting about the JS/TS version is that, by focusing on targeted mutants, mutation testing can become practical for E2E tests.

I took inspiration from SEMu, DSpot, the W-method, and Meta's ACH. I listed the links at the end.

Would love any feedback. Thanks for taking a look.

- Killing Stubborn Mutants with Symbolic Execution (SEMu): https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02941

- Automatic Test Improvement with DSpot: https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.08330

- Testing Software Design Modeled by Finite-State Machines (W-method): https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.1978.231496

- Mutation-Guided LLM-based Test Generation at Meta (ACH): https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12862

records.title: Show HN: Wots – restaurant recommendations from people with your taste
records.author: riverdweller
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I built Wots (Word on the Street) because star ratings have stopped helping me choose where to eat (or drink, or stay, etc.). Almost every place on places like Google Maps or similar has 4+ stars, and these averages have for too long revealed little about whether you will actually like it or not.

The idea with Wots is you rate a few places you know (just "loved it" or "not for me"). It then finds people whose ratings intersect with yours, your "taste twins", and shows you the places they love, anywhere on the map.

You can try it without an account (rate three places and the map starts recommending - though the more you rate the better the results should be). If you sign up (free but google only for now, sorry) you can get more recommendations, can save places as a reminder, etc.

It's early days, and the recommendations you get depend on how many people have rated places in your area of interest, so they're currently good in some cities and thin in many others. That's what I most want to improve. If you've travelled widely then your likes are particularly interesting, as it will give other people good tips across different countries!

I'd love feedback on whether the recommendations make sense for you, and on anything confusing in the first minute.

Built with Postgres/PostGIS (after an earlier Redis set-based approach that was fast but was not going to scale), if anyone's curious.

records.title: Show HN: Bloque – Hosted MCP gateway for teams without an IT department
records.author: k4200
records.storyText:
Bloque is a hosted MCP gateway for teams without an IT department. There are many MCP gateway products out there, but they are either overkill or too difficult to use. The pricing of a popular product starts at $500/mo, another one requires you to have your own infrastructure, and so on.

As the owner of a small company, I encourage my team members to use AI and MCP servers in their daily work, but don't want to waste time helping them set them up. I also need to manage and monitor how they use them.

With Bloque, I set up MCP servers once, issue API keys for my team members, and let them connect Claude, ChatGPT, or any tool of their choice to Bloque's single endpoint. That part is easy. Then, I can manage and monitor who calls which tool, when.

Bloque started as a fork of the MIT-licensed Plugged.in. We kept the MCP-related core, removed everything else, and rebuilt it as a multi-tenant hosted gateway.

Other features include: - Teams - Isolated runtime environments (where stdio-based servers run) - Per-user 3LO: each team member can call MCP servers with their own credentials - Enable/disable tools

It's a freemium service: - Free (shared runner, no MCP Playground) - Starter: $5/mo (shared runner) - Pro: $25/mo (dedicated runner) - Team: $29/mo includes 2 seats, $7/mo per additional seat (dedicated runner, team management)

I would love feedback, especially from our target audience: one-person IT admins at SMEs.

records.title: Show HN: Scolast – AI tutor for autodidacts inspired by Bloom's 2 sigma problem
records.author: PavleMiha
records.storyText:
I was using Claude to learn physics and I was getting a bit frustrated with the interface (I kept interrupting the conversation to get a quick explainer on something, and there was no good interface for Claude to ask me questions) so I built Scolast!

It's an AI tutor that follows Bloom's findings (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom%27s_2_sigma_problem) that 1 to 1 tutoring, using mastery learning (basically only moving ahead when the student has demonstrated they learned something, but also moving ahead as quickly as possible) can have pretty incredible results, around two standard deviations higher than regular classroom learning. Bloom called it a problem because this was obviously untenable - but it's actually possible now!

I also added little side explainers for anything that's confusing, plus worksheets, and I've been iterating on the voice of the tutor, to try to get a sort of Feynman-y focus on the whys and the experiments and experiences that motivated each piece of knowledge.

I find that it's quite remarkable, I'm actually retaining some of the physics I've never been able to retain in the past, and it seems useful in a lot of other domains - my wife used it for language learning and to pass a yoga exam; I've used it to learn some machine learning subjects, etc. One interesting side effect is that I find using it quite tiring, and I actually use tokens very slowly compared to agentic coding - when you actually have to read every token carefully you really get your money's worth.

Would love to get people's thoughts so I'm throwing in $3 in free tokens while my budget lasts. After that you can buy tokens and I'm charging an extra 10% to cover everything else. Eventually I'd like to hook it up to people's existing subscriptions, I've applied to OAI's program for this, waiting to see if Ant will offer it.

Cheers

records.title: Show HN: Sandbox platform on Kubernetes for secure remote access without secrets
records.author: geoctl
records.storyText:
Cordium is a FOSS, self-hosted, identity-based, general-purpose sandbox platform built on Kubernetes. The primary differentiator here is that Cordium automatically assigns an identity to each sandbox to provide "secretless" secure zero-trust remote access to resources/infrastructure (e.g. APIs, SSH, databases, k8s, etc.) without having to hold credentials and secrets (e.g. API keys and access tokens, SSH private keys/passwords, database passwords, mTLS private keys, etc.) inside the sandbox.

The way it works is that every Cordium sandbox includes an Octelium ZTNA client (see https://github.com/octelium/octelium) which routes requests from the sandbox to the upstream resources through the Octelium Cluster running on the same underlying Kubernetes cluster over WireGuard tunnels. In the Octelium Cluster, each upstream resource is protected by a corresponding identity-aware proxy that actually holds the upstream credential that injects the credential on-the-fly to the upstream if the downstream (i.e. the Cordium sandbox) is authorized by an Octelium policy.

In short, Cordium is basically a sandbox platform with a _dual nature_: it doesn't just provide isolated execution runtimes but it also provides and identity and access infrastructure to provide secure secretless remote access, identity management, L7-aware access control and visibility for every request originating from within the sandbox. You can use it for various use cases from a personal self-hosted GitHub Codespaces alternative for remote development as well as a scalable sandbox platform for AI agents to access infrastructure without handling them your credentials at scale. You can also use it as an infrastructure layer to build more complex applications such as agent meshes.

The primary features include declarative management, Templates and prebuilds, persistent, ephemeral and forkable storage via Kubernetes volume snapshots, lifecycle tasks, controls such as linux caps, read-only filesystem and egress control, access and management over web portal/SSH/CLI as well as SDKs in Go/Rust/Python/Typescript. You can learn more about Cordium, its features in detail and how it works, please visit the docs at https://octelium.com/docs/cordium/latest/overview/intro

You can also try a live demo for the Cordium web portal at https://demo.octelium.com/cordium and a CLI playground at https://demo.octelium.com/cli

records.title: Show HN: Yioop 10 – a PHP search engine that runs groups, wikis, Git and mail
records.author: cpollett
records.storyText:
Yioop is an open source (GPLv3) search engine written in PHP that I have been working on since 2009. Version 10 is now out.

Yioop comes with a crawler which can be used on the open web or on a list of sites you choose. It can also index Wikipedia XML dumps, arc and warc archives, Open Directory RDF, and dumps of email or databases, and several crawls can be mixed into one set of results. A media updater re-indexes RSS and Atom feeds every hour, so news makes it into the results.

Besides search, Yioop can be used to run discussion groups, blogs and wikis. Each group has a wiki for pages, slide presentations and spreadsheets, and the wiki can be used to build whole web sites.

Some of what is new in version 10: - Yioop can run on its own Pure PHP web server, with HTTPS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 support, and has its own web configurable PHP mail server and client. - Users can make voice and video calls from their messages. - Common audio and video formats are decoded and encoded in Yioop's own PHP code. - A wiki page can hold a git repository that people clone and push to over HTTP, with an issue tracker beside it. - Yioop is available in 25 languages, and a faster tokenizer handles text in each of them, including Chinese, Japanese and Korean.

Yioop's stemmers, summarizers and other language tools can also be used in other projects through Composer.

Demo: https://www.yioop.com/ Project page: https://www.seekquarry.com/
